strengths: Addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text decoding: overlapping stimuli and subjects can make reported performance misleading about generalization. A rigorous correction would be valuable independently of proposing a new model.

The distinction between subject overlap, stimulus overlap, and overlapping fMRI windows provides a useful framework for designing evaluations on unseen subjects and text. The diagrams make the intended splitting principles understandable.

Experiments cover two established models and both EEG and fMRI, with additional-test and shuffled-input controls. Table 6 also reports results without teacher forcing and shows that some performance differences persist, supporting a narrower concern about evaluation sensitivity.
weaknesses: The main evaluation is confounded by teacher forcing at inference. Tables 3–5, including the proposed 'fair benchmark,' use reference prefixes, as confirmed by Appendix E and Table 6. These results do not measure generation from brain signals alone, and access to reference prefixes particularly facilitates completion of memorized stimuli. Table 6 is useful, but the shuffled-input and additional-test controls must also be repeated without teacher forcing to substantiate the central decoding claims.

The supplied splitting algorithms do not enforce the stated guarantees. Algorithm 1, line 15, checks subject membership during expansion but does not exclude text assigned to validation/test, allowing stimulus overlap to return. Algorithm 2, line 33, checks story membership but omits the corresponding subject restriction. These conditions contradict the restrictions in the main formulation. Corrected pseudocode and an auditable implementation are necessary to establish that the experimental splits actually satisfy both constraints.

The mathematical definitions need correction. Equations 6–7 require every training example to overlap with a test example, although one overlapping pair suffices for leakage. Equation 17 intersects individual brain-signal records, which can remain disjoint despite subject overlap, making the reported BSLR values difficult to reconcile with its definition. Appendix D's assertion that discarding samples is unavoidable also requires additional assumptions: disconnected subject–stimulus components can be assigned intact to different splits.

The interpretation of overfitting is not adequately supported. Decreasing reconstruction validation loss in Figure 5 does not establish degraded encoder representations, and improving test performance with longer training is not itself evidence of leakage. Changing the split also changes subject/story distributions and the amount of retained training data. Evaluation on a common held-out population with controlled training sizes is needed to distinguish these effects.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the proposed benchmark. Although Appendix B gives some hyperparameters, the manuscript does not link code or split manifests, report post-filtering and per-split sample counts or discarded fractions, or adequately specify the additional test set and shuffling procedure. The asserted 80:10:10 allocation is not demonstrated after expansion and discarding. Only leakage rates receive multi-seed uncertainty estimates; decoding results lack uncertainty across runs or held-out subjects.

The claim that all existing splitting methods are wrong exceeds the evidence and conflates different evaluation targets. Jointly unseen subjects and stimuli constitute a useful generalization setting, but overlap is not automatically invalid when evaluating calibrated subjects or explicitly restricting evaluation to known stimuli. The paper should connect criticisms to each prior method's stated claims and narrow conclusions to the regimes and models actually examined.

Reported metrics contain consequential inconsistencies. Table 5 gives EEG2Text ROUGE-1 F=25.74 with P=23.95 and R=23.98, incompatible with standard consistently aggregated F1. The value 40.65 is labeled ROUGE-1 F in Table 3 but recall in Table 7. An audit of metric computation and table transcription, together with corrected splitting and generation-based controls, is needed before the contribution meets the soundness and reproducibility threshold for Findings.
